content_blocks.title: Core idea
content_blocks.text: A runtime matrix tests the supported language versions so compatibility problems surface before release. A useful CI pipeline gives a clear pass/fail result for relevant quality checks. Keep fast checks early, use services only when tests need them, and ensure required checks cannot be skipped accidentally. The most useful check is one that produces observable evidence and fails clearly when its stated requirement is not met.

items.title: Runtime version selection
items.text: Make the workflow contract explicit: identify the event, job runner, inputs, command/action, output, and failure signal. Keep steps small and review the permissions and source of every action.

items.title: Version matrices
items.text: Trace the release to a source commit, validate the selected version/ref, restrict publication permissions, retain build evidence, and verify the published artifact before promoting it.

items.title: Compatibility testing
items.text: Make the check deterministic and fail with a meaningful status when requirements are not met. Preserve reports where useful and configure required branch checks to match the checks the workflow actually emits.

items.title: Supported-version policies
items.text: Trace the release to a source commit, validate the selected version/ref, restrict publication permissions, retain build evidence, and verify the published artifact before promoting it.

items.title: Reproducing version-specific failures
items.text: Start with the first failed step and its exit code, then inspect the event, conditions, permissions, tool versions, network, and runner state. Capture sanitized diagnostics and preserve evidence of the failure.

content_blocks.code:
name: Runtime compatibility
on: [push, pull_request]
permissions:
  contents: read
jobs:
  test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    strategy:
      matrix:
        python-version: ["3.11", "3.12", "3.13"]
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-python@v6
        with:
          python-version: ${{ matrix.python-version }}
      - run: python -m pytest
content_blocks.expected_output: The same tests run on each configured interpreter, exposing version compatibility issues.
content_blocks.run_instructions: Confirm these interpreter versions are supported and install project test dependencies in the workflow.
content_blocks.reset_steps: Do not claim support for a version unless the application and dependency policy allow it.

items.title: Syntax and scope

items.title: Permissions and trust
items.text: Start with read-only access. If the example needs more access, explain the exact operation and reduce permissions again afterwards.

items.title: Evidence
items.text: Use the run summary and first failing step. A green result is meaningful only when the intended checks actually ran.

content_blocks.title: Recap
content_blocks.text: You should now be able to explain testing different language versions, read the example, and identify a way to validate it. The wider system goal remains: Build CI checks that produce repeatable evidence and protect merge quality.

content.expected_output: The expected result is the behavior described here: A runtime matrix tests the supported language versions so compatibility problems surface before release. The real result depends on the repository, selected ref, configured permissions, and runner availability.
troubleshooting: If a workflow never starts, verify the workflow is under `.github/workflows/`, the event and filters match, and repository/organization Actions policy allows it.
If a step fails, inspect the first failed step, exit code, stderr, installed tool versions, permissions, and runner/network state before retrying.
If a job is skipped or data is missing, inspect `if`, `needs`, outputs, artifact names/paths, and cache keys; jobs do not automatically share filesystems.
common_mistakes: Assuming YAML parsing proves the workflow runs correctly or matches the intended trigger.
Granting broad token permissions, printing environment values, or exposing a secret to untrusted code.
Using a placeholder command as evidence of a real build, test, deployment, or security scan.
